items.prompt: Explain how culture and position can influence women’s opportunities.
items.canonical_answer: Cultural values and practices influence expectations about work, property and participation. They can support cooperation or restrict opportunities depending on their form and use; culture is diverse and changing, not a fixed explanation of all women’s experiences.
marking_guidance: Reason: develop a link from an expectation or practice to access or voice, without treating all women’s experiences as identical.

items.prompt: Explain the participation effect in a fictional village where meetings occur during women’s allocated water-collection time and decisions proceed without their input.
items.canonical_answer: The timetable makes attendance conflict with an assigned task, so those affected lose an opportunity to influence decisions. Changing time or sharing the collection task could reduce that particular barrier.
marking_guidance: Mechanism: time conflict linked to missing input.
Consequence: restricted influence; no assumption of lack of interest.

items.prompt: Explain how taboos and myths can influence women’s opportunities.
items.canonical_answer: A taboo restricts an activity or discussion; a myth may be used to explain or justify a belief. items.prompt: Explain whether a fictional historical change establishes an overall improvement for women: wage work becomes available, but women lose food-growing access and retain the same unpaid workload. Judge livelihood choice and welfare.
items.canonical_answer: The wage opportunity may provide income, but reduced food access and unchanged unpaid burdens can offset it. An overall verdict needs earnings, food costs and workload evidence; wage availability alone does not establish improved choice or welfare.
marking_guidance: Judgement: weigh gains and losses against livelihood choice and welfare.
Reason: use all supplied changes and identify what evidence is missing.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe this fictional historical comparison: before a change, women hold 60% of household food plots and 10% of paid jobs; afterwards, 30% of plots and 25% of paid jobs.
items.canonical_answer: Paid-job participation rises 15 percentage points while plot control falls 30 points. The two access measures move in opposing directions, so more paid work does not establish wider access to all productive resources.
marking_guidance: Evidence: accurate paired changes.
Relationship: contrast paid opportunity and plot control.

items.prompt: State (a) two useful measures of women’s contribution beyond wages [2]. Explain (b) why a fictional change bringing paid jobs but removing food-growing access cannot be judged from job numbers alone [4].

Development: connect the opposing supplied changes to a bounded welfare judgement [4].

items.prompt: Describe (a) this fictional comparison: A offers training at 40% participation and meetings at 20%; B offers 70% and 60% [3]. Suggest (b) a priority for A if both timetable clashes and lack of care cover are reported and the aim is fair access [3].
items.canonical_answer: (a) B combines higher training and meeting participation, by 30 and 40 percentage points. (b) Arrange workable times and care support with affected participants, then monitor access; those changes address stated barriers rather than interpreting low participation as unwillingness.
marking_guidance: Evidence: paired participation comparisons [3].
Meaning: action matched to both barriers and the fair-access aim [3].
